TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
WEDNESDAY, 1 MARCH 2023 AT 9:58 AM (AEST)
DAY 39
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MR ANGUS SCOTT KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MR DOUGLAS FREEBURN, Counsel Assisting
MS SALWA MARSH, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR MICHAEL PRUSCINO, for the Commonwealth
MS ANNA CAPPELLANO, for Annette Musolino

COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Freeburn. Sorry, I will take the appearances for the day.
MR FREEBURN: Thank you, Commissioner. My name is Freeburn, initial D. I appear as
Counsel Assisting.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Ms Hogan-Doran?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Yes, Commissioner. I appear today with Mr Pruscino for the
Commonwealth.
COMMISSIONER: And Ms Cappellano?
MS CAPPELLANO: Thank you, Commissioner. I appear today instructed by Sparke Helmore
Lawyers for the witness Ms Musolino.
COMMISSIONER: Do you want a not-before time? Because I don't think we will start
Ms Musolino before 11 at the earlier earliest.
MS CAPPELLANO: Certainly, your Honour. Thank you.
COMMISSIONER: And are you on the premises? We can probably let you know.
MS CAPPELLANO: We are here, and that's fine. We might sit in for the first part but then
return before 11.
COMMISSIONER: I'm sorry, I didn't get the last bit. What?
MS CAPPELLANO: We will sit in for the first part and then we can return before 11.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. It certainly won't be any earlier than 11.
MS CAPPELLANO: Thank you.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. Thank you, Mr Freeburn.
MR FREEBURN: Thank you, Commissioner. I call Mr Matthew Thompson.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Mr Thompson, would you take an oath or an affirmation?
MR THOMPSON: Affirmation, please.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Can you stand up and we will get that delivered to you.
<MATTHEW CLARKE THOMPSON, AFFIRMED

COMMISSIONER: Thank you. You can take a seat. Yes, Mr Freeburn.
MR FREEBURN: Mr Thompson, can you tell the Commission your full name, please?
MR THOMPSON: Matthew Clarke Thompson.
MR FREEBURN: Where are you currently living?
MR THOMPSON: Snug in Tasmania, a little bit south of Hobart.
MR FREEBURN: Did you prepare a Statement in preparation for giving evidence in this Royal
Commission dated the 19th of February of 2023?
MR THOMPSON: Yes, I did.
MR FREEBURN: And in the preparation of your Statement, did you have regard to a range of
documents provided by Services Australia?
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: Commissioner, I tender the Statement of Mr Thompson and a number of
related documents, including NTG-0148 to Services Australia, the response to that Notice
and a number of attachments.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. I don't have an exhibit list. Thank you. So what numbers are we are
looking at, Mr Freeburn?
MR FREEBURN: They commence, Commissioner, in the draft exhibit list at Exhibit 6216 and
run through to Exhibit 6241.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, just for my friend, we have not been served with the
exhibit list. So I think my instructors, actually, are speaking with your instructors now. Thank
you.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. The documents bearing the numbers 6216 through to 6241 on that
list are admitted as exhibits. Thank you.
<EXHIBITS 6216 TO 6241 TENDERED AS PER THE EXHIBIT LIST
MR FREEBURN: Mr Thompson, you're currently 50 years of age. Is that right?
MR THOMPSON: That's correct. Yep.
MR FREEBURN: Are you currently employed?

MR FREEBURN: In your Statement, you refer to employment that you engaged in at the
Hobart Mercury newspaper.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: And I will ask you some questions about that employment in a moment. But
before I do, would you mind giving the Commission a brief outline of your work history prior
to that employment?
MR THOMPSON: Yes. So since I was 18, I have had 28 different roles - 28 different jobs,
hospitality, forestry, journalism or photojournalism, that kind of thing. So I've been on - yes,
I've had 28 different jobs. So all of them have been casual apart from two, I think.
MR FREEBURN: Alright. You describe, Mr Thompson, a history of mental health issues in your
Statement.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: Are you able to give the Commission a brief description of the nature of
those conditions?
MR THOMPSON: So I've been in and out of mental health services in Tasmania all my life. I
was first diagnosed with schizophrenia, then bipolar about a decade afterwards, but it's only
recently that I've been diagnosed with generalised anxiety disorder, with panic attacks. So
I've had a long mental health history, but it’s – I’ve finally been properly diagnosed and I'm
on good medication and - yeah.
MR FREEBURN: Alright. Historically, what can you say about the impact that those mental
health conditions have had on your ability to find and secure work?
MR THOMPSON: Depends on the severity. If it's just a mild bit of anxiety, I can do limited
hours. But anything over four days, I just - I can't really cope with it. I just - my anxiety is too
high, and I end up having to drink and all that kind of thing to feel human. Yeah.
MR FREEBURN: And so that's posed some difficulties in terms of you holding down
employment. Is that right?
MR THOMPSON: Yes. Yes.
MR FREEBURN: Alright. You also explained in your Statement that you are currently living on
a rural property outside of Hobart.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: Do you own that property?

MR THOMPSON: I do, but I'm paying off a loan to the bank. I owe $60,000 left on it.
MR FREEBURN: And since when have you been living there?
MR THOMPSON: It could be about 11 or 12 years by now.
MR FREEBURN: Alright. Can you describe that property to the Commission?
MR THOMPSON: It's - I bought it before the big rise, so I got it fairly cheaply. It's five and a
half acres of beautiful bushland on the Snug River, 300 metres of river frontage, ferns. And
it's just a beautiful place to be. It's just lovely. Yeah.
MR FREEBURN: You explain in your Statement that you live off the grid. What does that
mean?
MR THOMPSON: So I did have the option of hooking up to the grid, because the
telephone - well, a pole right outside my house. But that was three and a half grand, so I just
decided to go off grid, which means solar panels, a big battery bank, so I can run all my
energy needs from that.
MR FREEBURN: Alright.
MR THOMPSON: Save money. Yeah.
MR FREEBURN: Can you describe the relationship, if any, between your living off the grid in a
rural area and the management of your mental health conditions?
MR THOMPSON: I think it's been essential. There seems to be a push for people with
disabilities to get them to live in town, you know, and close to services and all that kind of
thing. I - it's better for - I get anxious in cities. I have to medicate myself, and I just find it just
helps me live a peaceful life.
MR FREEBURN: Mr Thompson, I'm going to draw your attention to the period 2011 to 2015.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: In your Statement, you describe engaging in employment with the Hobart
Mercury during that period.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: I understand that the Hobart Mercury is a newspaper. Is that right?
MR THOMPSON: That's correct, yes.
MR FREEBURN: Can you briefly outline the nature of your work with the Hobart Mercury?

MR THOMPSON: So I was a photographer - casual photographer. There was about 15 of us
when I first started, and I think about eight when I left. We did - a wide range of jobs -
political. You would get given a job list with about 10 jobs a day and I would drive around and
take photos, sometimes with journalists, sometimes not. But it was covering bushfires,
politics, everything that's in a newspaper.
MR FREEBURN: And were you employed in that role on a casual basis?
MR THOMPSON: Yes. Yes.
MR FREEBURN: Can you describe your financial situation during that 2011 to 2015 period?
MR THOMPSON: That would have been before I started working at the Mercury or - - -
MR FREEBURN: In your Statement, you describe that you were working at the Mercury for
the duration of that period.
MR THOMPSON: Yes. I was casual. They say you are only as good as your last photograph,
and sometimes I wasn't good and sometimes I was good. And being a casual, you just fill the
gaps of the full-timers kind of thing. Yeah.
MR FREEBURN: I understand that you were accessing Centrelink benefits in that period.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: Is that right?
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: And you explain in your Statement that you accessed Newstart Allowance on
occasion.
MR THOMPSON: Yeah.
MR FREEBURN: What would life have been like without your Newstart Allowance?
MR THOMPSON: I couldn't live. And I mean that in - I would have to sell up the block of land,
which is everything to me. It's - it's stopping me being - living in poverty when I get older. I've
put every - I've put so much into it. I have spent about $12,000 on a development application
and 50 or 60 thousand dollars over that 10-year period, just doing things like solar panels
and levelling and getting the site prepared and all that sort of thing. So I - it - I don't really
want to think about it, because I don't - I really don't know how I would go living in poverty
later on.
MR FREEBURN: Alright. You also described how you accessed Sickness Allowance in that
period I described earlier. Is that right?

MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: What was your reason for accessing the Sickness Allowance?
MR THOMPSON: It - it's a very stressful job. I've got to drive an hour and a half to and from
work in peak traffic. Sorry, what was the question again?
MR FREEBURN: What was your reasoning for accessing Sickness Allowance?
MR THOMPSON: That's right, yes. I was working very hard, sometimes seven days a week. I
was - I think it was in the middle of winter, so I was living in a caravan in the cold, showering
myself and then going to work and taking all these photos. The stress level got to me so
much of everything. And one morning I woke up and I vomited, and I couldn't get out of bed.
I was just - yes. I've been to psych wards three times on three different occasions, and I was
very close to being hospitalised. But living in that beautiful bush, it sort of - I could just calm
myself down and work through it.
MR FREEBURN: So you were accessing the Sickness Allowance - - -
MR THOMPSON: While I wasn't working.
MR FREEBURN: - - - by virtue of the conditions that you described earlier?
MR THOMPSON: Yes. Yes.
COMMISSIONER: And your employer would not have been paying you when you weren't at
work, I take it, since it was a casual job?
MR THOMPSON: Sorry, Commissioner?
COMMISSIONER: Your employer, the Hobart Mercury, wouldn't have paid you for your time
when you couldn't work?
MR THOMPSON: No, not at all. No.
MR FREEBURN: Whilst you were accessing those Centrelink benefits, did you understand that
you were under any obligations relating to the reporting or declaration of your income?
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: What can you describe what your understanding of those obligations was?
MR THOMPSON: So with any Centrelink benefit, you have to apply each fortnight and you
put down your fortnightly incomes - your income for whatever job you are doing.
MR FREEBURN: So you declare on a fortnightly basis the earnings - - -

MR THOMPSON: Yeah.
MR FREEBURN: - - - that you had received from, in this case, the Mercury?
MR THOMPSON: Yes. So even being on a pension, like I am now, I will have to declare any
money earned and they will reduce my pension probably. So - yes.
MR FREEBURN: And to the best of your recollection, do you think you discharged your
reporting obligations?
MR THOMPSON: Yes. I do. Yep.
MR FREEBURN: Have your health conditions - so you discussed earlier how your health
conditions had affected your ability to secure employment.
MR THOMPSON: Yep.
MR FREEBURN: Have your health conditions affected your ability to deal with Centrelink?
MR THOMPSON: Yes. Definitely. With my mental health history, I've been on Centrelink since
I was very young, like 20 or something or rather. It was quite - it was easier back then. There
were more face to face and there was more humanity, I guess. These days - I've been on the
phone to them for hours. Sometimes you've got to wait three hours, and sometimes they
actually hang up on you. So to make a phone call, I need to do it in the afternoon after I've
medicated myself well enough so that I can just cope with whatever bad news they are going
to give me. And as for going into the office, I need to medicate myself quite a bit to just be
able to cope with being in there. It's - it's a symptom of generalised anxiety disorder, I guess.
It's just - I don't like crowds, that kind of thing. So dealing with Centrelink - it's a full-time job
being on Centrelink.
MR FREEBURN: Could the following document please be brought up by the operator. It's
Exhibit 6219. It's Doc ID CTH. - there it is. CTH.3822.0002.0008. I think that might be the
wrong document. Exhibit 6219. And, Mr Thompson, it should be behind your tab 4 in the
bundle in front of you. Mr Thompson, this is a letter dated 11 September of 2017, and it's
addressed to you by the agency. I will refer to this as the initial notice. Do you recognise this
document?
MR THOMPSON: Yes, I do.
MR FREEBURN: Do you recall receiving this notice at some point in or around September of
2017?
MR THOMPSON: Yes, I do.
MR FREEBURN: Now, by this initial notice, the agency asserts that it has identified some
discrepancy between the annual income information provided by the ATO and the amounts

document to confirm or update your income information within 28 days of receipt of the
initial notice?
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: Could the third page of this document please be shown. You see here the
notice then describes your total earnings for the three financial years commencing 2011 for
an employer named Davies Brothers Proprietary Limited.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: Do you recognise the name of that employer?
MR THOMPSON: Yes. That's - it's - Davies Brothers is the same as The Mercury, same as
News Corp, News Limited. They are all the same company.
MR FREEBURN: Alright. Can you describe to the Commission your reaction to receiving this
initial notice?
MR THOMPSON: I probably would have been on the way to work, because I pick up my mail
at the post office. I probably could have opened it and just put it away. I was really - it just
shocked me. And I had to go to work, and I can't - I can't really work properly with all that
going on in your head. So I just put it to one side. And I think I read it when I got back from
work, just to double-check. But it was just a complete shock and - - -
MR FREEBURN: And given your earlier evidence about the accuracy of your income
reporting, did you have any understanding as to how the agency had identified the
discrepancy that they outlined in the letter?
MR THOMPSON: No. No. No.
MR FREEBURN: The initial notice asked that you confirm or update your income information,
and we will discuss the debt notices in a moment. But prior to the raising of any debt, do you
recall whether you provided any information to Centrelink?
MR THOMPSON: I think I did, yes. Yes.
MR FREEBURN: Right.
MR THOMPSON: It would have been payslips from News Corp. Yeah.
MR FREEBURN: In your Statement, you outline that you provided some information after the
debts had been raised.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.

MR FREEBURN: Could it be the case that you also provided some information before the
debts had been raised?
MR THOMPSON: Possibly, yes. Yes.
COMMISSIONER: What did you actually do? I mean, did you get online or what - do you
remember?
MR THOMPSON: I think I probably would have rung them first. Yeah.
COMMISSIONER: And can you remember that or - it's okay if you can't. It's a while ago.
MR THOMPSON: I can vaguely remember it, but - yeah.
MR FREEBURN: Now, Mr Thompson, I now wish to bring to your attention two documents.
The first is Exhibit 6222, Doc ID CTH.3822.0002.0050. That's behind tab 7 of your bundle.
This is a letter dated 3 July 2018, and it's addressed to you by the agency. Do you recognise
that correspondence?
MR THOMPSON: Have we got the same ones or - - -
COMMISSIONER: Sorry, which tab are we in?
MR FREEBURN: Tab 7. Sorry, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Are you calling that a letter? It looks like an account payable.
MR FREEBURN: An account payable, sorry. Yes. So this is a notice that was sent to you that's
dated the 3rd of July of 2018. Do you recognise that document?
MR THOMPSON: Yes, I do. Yep.
MR FREEBURN: And do you recall receiving this notice at some point in July of 2018?
MR THOMPSON: Yes. Yep.
MR FREEBURN: The correspondence indicates that a debt in the amount of $5,352.94 is
payable by 1 August of 2018. And the debt is said to be raised in relation to the period - I
think it's 28 April 2012 to 26 October of 2012. And, significantly, the debt concerns your
Newstart Allowance.
MR THOMPSON: Yes. Yep.
MR FREEBURN: The notice also indicates that a recovery fee in the amount of just under
$500 was added to your debt on the grounds that quote:

The second document I wish to bring to your attention, Mr Thompson, is Exhibit 6223,
CTH.3822.0002.0051.
COMMISSIONER: Which is the next tab. I think you've got it.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: Do you recognise this notice?
MR THOMPSON: Yes, I do. Yes. It came on the same day, I think.
MR FREEBURN: Okay. Now, this correspondence indicates that you - sorry, that a debt
had - in the amount of $6,011 had been - was payable on 1 August of 2018.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: And the debt is said to be raised in relation to the period 9 July 2014 to 6
January 2015, and it's said to concern your Sickness Allowance. Do you see that?
MR THOMPSON: Yes. Yes.
MR FREEBURN: And like the debt - Newstart debt notice that we saw a moment ago, this
notice indicates that a recovery fee has also been added to this debt.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: So ultimately the effect of these notices is that you had debts in - totalling a
bit over $11,000 raised against you.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: Can you explain to the Commission your reaction to receiving these notices?
MR THOMPSON: Complete shock. I've put everything I possibly can into this block of land.
Every spare cent I've put in. And for - to get these two, it - it puts my progress back if they go
through with it. If they - I do have to pay them $11,000, that would set me back years and
years and years. I was shocked. I was - everything, angry, hurt, the whole thing. To the point
where I just had to put it aside and just not deal with it for a while. I can't remember
how - that might have been weeks or - yes.
MR FREEBURN: What can you say about the effects that the debts had on your mental
health?
MR THOMPSON: From a generalised anxiety disorder point of view, it's just a - the biggest
trigger you can give to somebody. Yes. Sorry, what was the question again?

MR FREEBURN: What was the effect of the debt notices on your mental health?
MR THOMPSON: My anxiety went through the roof. It then puts pressure on my
performance at work because you've got this thing in your head, you know, what are they
going to do, you know, take it out of my tax return or take out of my wages or - it just
shocked me very much.
MR FREEBURN: Given your financial position at the time, could you have afforded to service
or pay off the debts?
MR THOMPSON: No. Well, at a rate of about 50 bucks a week, I might be able to do it,
whatever that - however many years that would be to take - pay off.
MR FREEBURN: At the time, did you have any idea or appreciation as to how the agency had
calculated the debts?
MR THOMPSON: No. No. Not at all.
MR FREEBURN: Mr Thompson, I wish to show you a document, the significance of which will
become - or may become clearer later in your evidence. Could the witness be shown Exhibit
6218. It's at tab 3 of your bundle. It's CTH.9999.0001.0112.
COMMISSIONER: That's the notice?
MR FREEBURN: This is the response by the agency to - - -
COMMISSIONER: Okay.
MR FREEBURN: - - - the notice, NTG-0148. Could paragraph 1.11 be called out. It's on page 4.
And by this paragraph of the response, the agency makes clear that both the Newstart
Allowance debt and the Sickness Allowance debt amounts were initially determined on the
basis of averaging, that is, the apportionment of your annual income over the relevant
fortnightly periods. You understand that?
MR THOMPSON: Yes. Yep.
COMMISSIONER: I don't think we've got the sickness benefit bit up. That's it.
MR FREEBURN: Mr Thompson, were you aware that your debts had been calculated in this
way at the time?
MR THOMPSON: No. Not at all.
MR FREEBURN: And it's only in your preparations for giving evidence at this Royal
Commission that you have become aware of these matters?

COMMISSIONER: And this is probably an obvious question, but presumably you weren't
working regular hours every week? You didn't have a standard pattern of income?
MR THOMPSON: No. No, I didn't. My managers and bosses and everyone at The Mercury
were really lovely. They were very supportive of me. They have had people with mental
illness been through there before. Sorry, what was the next question again?
COMMISSIONER: It was just this: you weren't getting a fixed income each week, so you got
exactly the same each week; you were doing different hours. Am I correct?
MR THOMPSON: My manager - we had a good relationship. I said, "Look, I can't work five
days a week because of my illness.” And they were very good. If I wanted three, they would
give me three. If I wanted six, I could get six. But as you say, that fluctuated a lot.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR THOMPSON: And as you said before, when I - if I don't work, I don't get paid. So - - -
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Okay.
MR FREEBURN: I won't take you to this part of your Statement, but at a point in your
Statement you describe how you engaged in a telephone conversation with a representative
of the agency in August of 2018. And in that conversation, you say that you sought a review
of your debts. Do you recall doing that?
MR THOMPSON: Yes. Yep.
MR FREEBURN: Why did you do that?
MR THOMPSON: I asked for a review because it wasn't right. And I was lucky enough to
have - a lot of people with Robodebts don't have records going back, but I was lucky enough
to have been working for a corporation where they have got a head office where they have
got all my records. So I got them and I - - -
MR FREEBURN: When you say "records", what were those records?
MR THOMPSON: Payslips and tax and all your earnings.
MR FREEBURN: And did you subsequently provide those payslips to the agency?
MR THOMPSON: Yes. Yes.
MR FREEBURN: You will recall that the debts had been raised in respect of periods in 2012
and also in 2014 to 2015.

MR FREEBURN: And you describe in your Statement how you - on this occasion, in August of
2018, you only provided payslips for the period October 2014 to February 2015 initially.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Why did you not also provide payslip information for the 2012 period?
MR THOMPSON: It's a massive undertaking. I had - in my little house, I had all the payslips I
had, and I was working it out week by week. So I - because I had two debts, I decided to cut
my work in half. I just tried to prove them wrong with the first debt. And then if they are
wrong with that, then surely they - they should wipe the other one as well - yes.
MR FREEBURN: Alright. Could Exhibit 6230 please be brought up by the operator. It's at tab
15 of your bundle, Mr Thompson. CTH.3822.0002.0054. Mr Thompson, do you recognise this
correspondence?
MR THOMPSON: Yes, I do. Yep.
MR FREEBURN: This is a letter dated 18 April of 2019. And, again, it's addressed to you by the
agency. Do you recall receiving this notice at some - or this correspondence at some point in
April of 2019?
MR THOMPSON: Yes, I do. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Now, you will see by this correspondence, the agency indicates to you that
as a result of the information that you have provided, the Sickness Allowance debt had been
reduced from the $6,000 figure to $1,127. Do you see that?
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: The agency also indicates in that letter that because you hadn't provided
information relevant to your - relevant to the Newstart Allowance debt period, that debt had
remained unchanged.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: What was your reaction to receiving this correspondence?
MR THOMPSON: I was a little bit relieved, but "little" is - I was hoping that I was going to get
down, but - getting the debt down, but it's not much of a - it didn't make me feel very good
at all, really. Like, it's still wrong. I - so I guess I was a little bit pleased, but I still had the other
$5,000 they wanted from me anyway. So - - -
MR FREEBURN: Alright. And what was your attitude toward the debt - Newstart Allowance
debt remaining unchanged?

MR THOMPSON: It just doesn't - it didn't make sense to me. Yeah, it just doesn't - didn't
make sense to me.
MR FREEBURN: Alright. Now, Mr Thompson, I want to take you back to the Services Australia
response that I showed you earlier.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: Again, Exhibit 6218. Again, it's at tab 3 of your bundle. I'm going to take you
to paragraph 1.20 on page 6.
MR THOMPSON: 6. Which paragraph, sorry?
MR FREEBURN: 1.20.
MR THOMPSON: Yes, yes.
MR FREEBURN: Now, subparagraphs (a) and (b) indicate there that the re-assessment of your
Sickness Allowance debt was undertaking using information you supplied on the 16th of
October of 2018. Is that - is that - was that the occasion that we discussed earlier where you
provided - - -
MR THOMPSON: Yes, it was. Yes.
MR FREEBURN: Okay. And it says that the payslip information that you had provided enabled
the debt to be recalculated using only verified employment income and removed any
averaged ATO income information. Do you see that?
MR THOMPSON: Yes. Yes.
MR FREEBURN: Now, subparagraph (f) indicates the Newstart Allowance debt, bearing the
debt ID that appears there, was not re-assessed as you had not provided any information or
payslips for the period 28 April 2012 to 26 October 2012.
MR THOMPSON: Yep.
MR FREEBURN: Again, Mr Thompson, were you aware of these matters - the matters
described in that response at the time of your re-assessment?
MR THOMPSON: No. No.
MR FREEBURN: Or more accurately, at the time you were notified of the results of the
re-assessment?
MR THOMPSON: Sorry, can you ask the question again? Sorry.

MR FREEBURN: I'm just asking at the time you were notified that your debt had been
changed - your Sickness Allowance debt had been changed, were you aware of the matters
outlined in that paragraph?
MR THOMPSON: No. No.
MR FREEBURN: You also describe at paragraph 49 of your Statement that you subsequently
provided some further information to Centrelink.
MR THOMPSON: Yep.
MR FREEBURN: If that could be brought up, please. It's Exhibit 6216. Thank you. And so this
is - as I understand it, after the - you had been notified of the result of the re-assessment in
relation to your Sickness Allowance debt and you - is it the case that you attended on the 3rd
of June 2019 the - Centrelink's offices and provided some further information?
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: What was that information?
MR THOMPSON: Sorry, can you ask that one again.
MR FREEBURN: So what was the information that you provided Centrelink on this second
occasion?
MR THOMPSON: More payslips.
MR FREEBURN: More payslips.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
MR FREEBURN: And were those payslips relevant to the Newstart Allowance debt?
MR THOMPSON: They probably would have been. It would have been the one I was trying to
fight, I guess.
MR FREEBURN: Okay.
MR THOMPSON: And I got them all printed out on a great big sheet of paper and went into
Centrelink with them.
MR FREEBURN: Right.
MR THOMPSON: Yes.
